      <content name="title"><span class="qt0">Abdominal</span> Pain</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Bellyache</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Pain, <span class="qt0">Abdominal</span></content>
      <content name="altTitle"><span class="qt0">Stomach</span> Ache</content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>Your <span class="qt0">abdomen</span> extends from below your chest to your groin. Some people call it the <span class="qt0">stomach</span>, but your <span class="qt0">abdomen</span> contains many other important organs. Pain in the <span class="qt0">abdomen</span> can come from any one of them. The pain may start somewhere else, such as your chest. Severe pain doesn't always mean a serious problem. Nor does mild pain mean a problem is not serious. </p><p>Call your health care provider if mild pain lasts a week or more or if you have pain with other symptoms. Get medical help immediately if:</p><ul><li>	You have <span class="qt0">abdominal</span> pain that is sudden and sharp</li><li>You also have pain in your chest, neck or shoulder </li><li>	You're vomiting blood or have blood in your stool </li><li>	Your <span class="qt0">abdomen</span> is stiff, hard and tender to touch </li><li>You can't move your bowels, especially if you're also vomiting </li></ul></content>

      <content name="title">Appendicitis</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>The appendix is a small, tube-like organ attached to the first part of the large intestine. It is located in the lower right part of the <span class="qt0">abdomen</span>. It has no known function. A blockage inside of the appendix causes appendicitis. The blockage leads to increased pressure, problems with blood flow, and inflammation. If the blockage is not treated, the appendix can burst and spread infection into the <span class="qt0">abdomen</span>. This causes a condition called peritonitis.</p><p>The main symptom is pain in the <span class="qt0">abdomen</span>, often on the right side.  It is usually sudden and gets worse over time.  Other symptoms may include:</p><ul><li>	Swelling in the <span class="qt0">abdomen</span></li><li>	Loss of appetite</li><li>	Nausea and vomiting</li><li>	Constipation or diarrhea</li><li>	Inability to pass gas</li><li>	Low fever </li></ul><p>Not everyone with appendicitis has all these symptoms.</p><p>Appendicitis is a medical emergency. Treatment almost always involves removing the appendix. Anyone can get appendicitis, but it is more common among people 10 to 30 years old.</p><p>NIH: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases</p></content>

    <document rank="2" url="https://medlineplus.gov/aorticaneurysm.html">
      <content name="title">Aortic Aneurysm</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">AAA</content>
      <content name="altTitle"><span class="qt0">Abdominal</span> Aortic Aneurysm</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Aortic Dissection</content>
      <content name="altTitle">TAA</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Thoracic Aortic Aneurysm</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is an aortic aneurysm?<p>An aneurysm is a balloon-like bulge in the wall of an artery. Arteries are blood vessels that carry oxygen-rich blood from the heart to other parts of your body. Most aneurysms occur in the aorta, the main artery that runs from the heart through the chest and <span class="qt0">abdomen</span>.</p><p>If an aneurysm grows large, it can burst (rupture) or cause a tear in the artery wall (dissection). Both can lead to bleeding inside the body and be life-threatening.</p>What are the types of aortic aneurysms?<p>There are two types of aortic aneurysm:</p><ul><li><span class="qt0">Abdominal</span> aortic aneurysms (AAA) occur in the part of the aorta that runs through your <span class="qt0">abdomen (belly</span>). This is the most common type.</li><li>Thoracic aortic aneurysms (TAA) occur in the part of the aorta that runs through your chest.</li></ul>What causes an aortic aneurysm?<p>Aortic aneurysms develop when the aortic wall weakens over time. Sometimes the exact cause is unknown. Possible causes may include:</p><ul><li>Atherosclerosis (a buildup of fat and other substances in the arteries)</li><li>Injury to the aorta</li><li>Certain infections, such as syphilis</li><li>Certain genetic conditions</li></ul>What increases the risk of an aortic aneurysm?<p>Factors that may increase your risk of an aortic aneurysm include:</p><ul><li>Smoking</li><li>High blood pressure</li><li>High cholesterol</li><li>Family history of aneurysms</li><li>Being male (higher risk for <span class="qt0">abdominal</span> aortic aneurysm)</li><li>Older age (higher risk for <span class="qt0">abdominal</span> aortic aneurysm)</li><li>Being white (higher risk for <span class="qt0">abdominal</span> aortic aneurysm)</li></ul>What are the symptoms of an aortic aneurysm?<p>Most aortic aneurysms don't cause symptoms. If you do have symptoms, they may depend on where the aneurysm is and whether it has become large enough to affect other parts of your body. Possible symptoms may include:</p><ul><li>Painful or difficulty swallowing</li><li>A pulsing or throbbing feeling in your <span class="qt0">abdomen (belly</span>)</li><li>Pain in the neck, jaw, back, chest, shoulder, or <span class="qt0">abdomen (belly</span>)</li><li>Shortness of breath or trouble breathing</li><li>Swelling of the face, neck, or arms</li></ul><p>If an aneurysm breaks open it is called a rupture. A ruptured aortic aneurysm can cause sudden, severe internal bleeding and is a medical emergency. Call 911 right away if you have:</p><ul><li>Sudden, severe pain in your <span class="qt0">abdomen (belly</span>), chest, or back</li><li>Dizziness</li><li>A fast heartbeat</li></ul>How is an aortic aneurysm diagnosed?<p>A health care provider may find aneurysms during tests done for other health issues. To check for an aortic aneurysm, your provider may:</p><ul><li>Do a physical exam</li><li>Order imaging tests such as an ultrasound, to find or measure an aneurysm</li><li>Order a CT scan, or MRI scan for more details about the shape or location of an aneurysm</li><li>Order an echocardiogram to check the size of the aneurysm and the thoracic aorta, which is close to the heart</li></ul>Who should be screened for an aortic aneurysm?<p>Because aneurysms often don't cause symptoms, screening is important if you are at higher risk. Talk to your provider to see whether screening is right for you. In general, screening for an aortic aneurysm is usually done with an ultrasound.</p><p>Screening for an <span class="qt0">abdominal</span> aortic aneurysm is recommended for:</p><ul><li>Men 65 to 75 years old who have smoked or have a close relative with an aortic aneurysm</li><li>Men 65 to 75 years old who have never smoked but have other risk factors, such as family history, other aneurysms, or coronary artery disease</li><li>Men and women older than 75 years old who have smoked or have a close relative with an aneurysm</li><li>People with peripheral artery disease may also need screening</li></ul><p>Your provider may recommend screening for a thoracic aortic aneurysm if you have:</p><ul><li>A close relative with a thoracic aortic aneurysm</li><li>Certain genetic conditions such as Marfan syndrome, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, Loeys-Dietz syndrome, or Turner syndrome </li></ul>What are the treatments for an aortic aneurysm?<p>Treatment for an aortic aneurysm depends on its size and how fast it's growing. The treatment options may include heart-healthy lifestyle changes, medicines, and surgery.</p><ul><li>Small aneurysms are often monitored with regular imaging tests and treated with medicines to manage blood pressure and cholesterol</li><li>Large or fast-growing aneurysms often require surgery to reduce the risk of rupture</li></ul>Can an aortic aneurysm be prevented?<p>You may not be able to prevent an aortic aneurysm, but you can lower your risk by:</p><ul><li>Not smoking (or quitting smoking)</li><li>Managing your blood pressure and cholesterol</li><li>Eating a heart-healthy diet</li><li>Getting regular physical activity</li><li>Managing stress</li><li>Knowing your family history and asking your provider about screening</li></ul><p>NIH: National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute</p></content>

    <document rank="3" url="https://medlineplus.gov/crohnsdisease.html">
      <content name="title">Crohn's Disease</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Ileocolitis</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Inflammatory Bowel Disease</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Regional Enteritis</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Regional Ileitis</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is Crohn's disease?<p>Crohn's disease is a chronic (long-lasting) disease that causes inflammation in your digestive tract. It can affect any part of your digestive tract, which runs from your mouth to your anus. But it usually affects your small intestine and the beginning of your large intestine.</p><p>Crohn's disease is an inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). Ulcerative colitis and microscopic colitis are other common types of IBD.</p>What causes Crohn's disease?<p>The cause of Crohn's disease is unknown. Researchers think that an autoimmune reaction may be one cause. An autoimmune reaction happens when your immune system attacks healthy cells in your body. Genetics may also play a role, since Crohn's disease can run in families.</p><p>Stress and eating certain foods don't cause the disease, but they can make your symptoms worse.</p>Who is more likely to develop Crohn's disease?<p>There are certain factors that may raise your risk of Crohn's disease:</p><ul><li>Family history of the disease. Having a parent, child, or sibling with the disease puts you at higher risk.</li><li>Smoking. This may double your risk of developing Crohn's disease.</li><li>Certain medicines, such as antibiotics, birth-control pills, and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) such as aspirin or ibuprofen. These may slightly increase your chance of developing Crohn's.</li><li>A high-fat diet. This may also slightly increase your risk of Crohn's.</li></ul>What are the symptoms of Crohn's disease?<p>The symptoms of Crohn's disease can vary, depending where and how severe your inflammation is. The most common symptoms include:</p><ul><li>Diarrhea</li><li>Cramping and pain in your <span class="qt0">abdomen</span></li><li>Weight loss</li></ul><p>Some other possible symptoms are:</p><ul><li>Anemia, a condition in which you have fewer red blood cells than normal</li><li>Eye redness or pain</li><li>Fatigue</li><li>Fever</li><li>Joint pain or soreness</li><li>Nausea or loss of appetite</li><li>Skin changes that involve red, tender bumps under the skin</li></ul><p>Stress and eating certain foods such as carbonated (fizzy) drinks and high-fiber foods may make some people's symptoms worse.</p>What other problems can Crohn's disease cause?<p>Crohn's disease can cause other problems, including:</p><ul><li>Intestinal obstruction, a blockage in the intestine</li><li>Fistulas, abnormal connections between two parts inside of the body</li><li>Abscesses, pus-filled pockets of infection</li><li>Anal fissures, small tears in your anus that may cause itching, pain, or bleeding</li><li>Ulcers, open sores in your mouth, intestines, anus, or perineum</li><li>Malnutrition, when your body does not get the right amount of vitamins, minerals, and nutrients it needs</li><li>Inflammation in other areas of your body, such as your joints, eyes, and skin</li></ul>How is Crohn's disease diagnosed?<p>Your health care provider may use many tools to make a diagnosis:</p><ul><li>A medical history, which includes asking about your symptoms</li><li>A family history</li><li>A physical exam, including:
	<ul><li>Checking for bloating in your <span class="qt0">abdomen</span>.</li><li>Listening to sounds within your <span class="qt0">abdomen</span> using a stethoscope.</li><li>Tapping on your <span class="qt0">abdomen</span> to check for tenderness and pain and to see if your liver or spleen is abnormal or enlarged.</li></ul>
</li><li>Various tests, including:
	<ul><li>Blood and stool tests.</li><li>A colonoscopy.</li><li>An upper GI endoscopy, a procedure in which your provider uses a scope to look inside your mouth, esophagus, <span class="qt0">stomach</span>, and small intestine.</li><li>Diagnostic imaging tests, such as a CT scan or an upper GI series. An upper GI series uses a special liquid called barium and x-rays. Drinking the barium will make your upper GI tract more visible on an x-ray.</li></ul>
</li></ul>What are the treatments for Crohn's disease?<p>There is no cure for Crohn's disease, but treatments can decrease inflammation in your intestines, relieve symptoms, and prevent complications. Treatments include medicines, bowel rest, and surgery. No single treatment works for everyone. You and your provider can work together to figure out which treatment is best for you:</p><ul><li>Medicines for Crohn's include various medicines that decrease the inflammation. Many of these medicines do this by reducing the activity of your immune system. Certain medicines can also help with symptoms or complications, such as nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and anti-diarrheal medicines. If your Crohn's causes an infection, you may need antibiotics.</li><li>Bowel rest involves drinking only certain liquids or not eating or drinking anything. This allows your intestines to rest. You may need to do this if your Crohn's disease symptoms are severe. You get your nutrients through drinking a liquid, a feeding tube, or an intravenous (IV) tube. You may need to do bowel rest in the hospital, or you may be able to do it at home. It will last for a few days or up to several weeks.</li><li>Surgery can treat complications and reduce symptoms when other treatments are not helping enough. The surgery will involve removing a damaged part of your digestive tract to treat:
	<ul><li>Fistulas</li><li>Bleeding that is life threatening</li><li>Intestinal obstructions</li><li>Side effects from medicines when they threaten your health</li><li>Symptoms when medicines do not improve your condition</li></ul>
</li></ul><p>Changing your diet can help reduce symptoms. Your provider may recommend that you make changes to your diet, such as:</p><ul><li>Avoiding carbonated drinks</li><li>Avoiding popcorn, vegetable skins, nuts, and other high-fiber foods</li><li>Drinking more liquids</li><li>Eating smaller meals more often</li><li>Keeping a food diary to help identify foods that cause problems</li></ul><p>In some cases, your provider may ask you to go on a special diet, such as a diet that is:</p><ul><li>High calorie</li><li>Lactose free</li><li>Low fat</li><li>Low fiber</li><li>Low salt</li></ul><p>If you are not absorbing enough nutrients, you may need to take nutritional supplements and vitamins.</p><p>NIH: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases</p></content>

    <document rank="4" url="https://medlineplus.gov/refluxinchildren.html">
      <content name="title">Reflux in Children</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">GERD in Children</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Gastroesophageal Reflux in Children</content>
      <content name="altTitle">GER in Children</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is reflux (GER) and GERD?<p>Gastroesophageal reflux (GER), often called reflux, occurs when food or <span class="qt0">stomach</span> acid flows back from your child's <span class="qt0">stomach</span> into the esophagus. The esophagus is the tube that carries food from your mouth to your <span class="qt0">stomach</span>. This can sometimes cause irritation or a burning sensation. Occasional reflux is common and usually not a problem.</p><p>Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) is a more serious and long-lasting type of reflux. GERD can cause repeated symptoms or damage to the lining of the esophagus. Having reflux two or more times a week may be a sign of GERD. Your child's health care provider may diagnose GERD if the reflux causes pain, feeding problems, or irritation of the esophagus.</p>What causes reflux and GERD in children?<p>A small muscle called the lower esophageal sphincter acts as a valve between the esophagus and <span class="qt0">stomach</span>. When your child swallows, this muscle relaxes to let food pass from the esophagus to the <span class="qt0">stomach</span>. This muscle normally stays closed, so the <span class="qt0">stomach</span> contents and acid don't flow back into the esophagus. This muscle, along with the diaphragm (the large muscle between the chest and <span class="qt0">abdomen</span>), usually prevents reflux. It's normal for children to have reflux occasionally.</p><p>In children who have GERD, the lower esophageal sphincter may be weak or relax when it shouldn't. That allows <span class="qt0">stomach</span> contents into the esophagus. This can happen because of:</p><ul><li>A hiatal hernia, a condition in which the upper part of the <span class="qt0">stomach</span> pushes up into the chest</li><li>Increased pressure on the <span class="qt0">abdomen (belly</span>) from being overweight or having obesity</li><li>Certain medicines, such as some used to treat asthma, allergies, depression, or pain</li><li>Smoking or exposure to secondhand smoke</li><li>Previous surgery on the esophagus or upper <span class="qt0">abdomen</span></li><li>Developmental delays or certain neurological conditions, such as cerebral palsy</li><li>Lung conditions, such as cystic fibrosis</li></ul>How common are reflux and GERD in children?<p>Many children have occasional reflux, especially after large meals or physical activity. GERD is less common, and most symptoms improve with time and lifestyle changes. </p>What are the symptoms of reflux and GERD in children?<p>Symptoms may vary by age. Some children might not even notice reflux, while others may taste food or <span class="qt0">stomach</span> acid in the back of their mouth.</p><p>In children, GERD can cause:</p><ul><li>Heartburn, a burning feeling in the chest or throat (more common in older children and teens)</li><li>Bad breath</li><li>Nausea or vomiting</li><li>Trouble or pain when swallowing</li><li>Cough, hoarseness, or breathing problems</li><li>Wearing away of tooth enamel from <span class="qt0">stomach</span> acid</li></ul><p>Other conditions can cause similar symptoms. Talk to your child's provider if symptoms happen often or make eating, sleeping, or daily activities difficult.</p>How are reflux and GERD diagnosed in children?<p>In most cases, your child's provider can tell if it's reflux by learning about your child's symptoms and health history. Tests are usually needed only if symptoms don't get better with lifestyle changes or medicines, or if another health problem is suspected.</p><p>Common tests include:</p><ul><li>Upper GI series, which looks at the shape of your child's upper GI (gastrointestinal) tract. Your child will drink or eat a chalky-tasting liquid called barium. For young children, the barium is mixed in with a bottle or other food. Several x-rays are taken to track the barium as it goes through your child's esophagus and <span class="qt0">stomach</span>.</li><li>Esophageal pH and impedance monitoring, which measures the amount of acid or liquid in your child's esophagus. A thin flexible tube is placed through their nose into the <span class="qt0">stomach</span>. The end of the tube in the esophagus measures when and how much acid comes up into the esophagus. The other end of the tube attaches to a monitor that records the measurements. Your child will wear the tube for 24 hours. They may need to stay in the hospital during the test.</li><li>Upper gastrointestinal (GI) endoscopy and biopsy, which uses an endoscope, a long, flexible tube with a light and camera at the end of it. An endoscope is inserted down your child's esophagus, <span class="qt0">stomach</span>, and first part of the small intestine. While looking at the pictures from the endoscope, tissue samples (biopsy) may be taken.</li></ul>What lifestyle changes can help treat my child's reflux or GERD?<p>Simple lifestyle changes can often improve symptoms. Examples include:</p><ul><li>Maintaining a healthy weight.</li><li>Eating smaller meals.</li><li>Avoiding high-fat foods or other trigger foods that cause symptoms.</li><li>Wearing loose-fitting clothing around the <span class="qt0">abdomen (belly</span>).</li><li>Staying upright for 3 hours after meals and avoiding slouching when sitting.</li><li>Sleeping with the head of the bed raised 6 to 8 inches.</li></ul>What are the treatments for my child's GERD?<p>If lifestyle changes aren't enough, your provider may recommend medicine to reduce <span class="qt0">stomach</span> acid. The medicines work by lowering the amount of acid your child's <span class="qt0">stomach</span> makes. Some are available over-the-counter, while others need a prescription. Do not give your child any medicine unless your provider recommends it.</p><p>If symptoms don't get better or are severe, your provider may refer you to a doctor who treats <span class="qt0">stomach</span> and digestion problems in children. In rare cases, surgery may be considered.</p><p>If GERD isn't treated, it can cause problems such as inflammation or scarring in the esophagus, changes in its lining (Barrett's esophagus), or make breathing problems, like asthma, worse.</p><p>NIH: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases</p></content>
